description: Rolling roster of must-read articles on AI and labor markets. Updated weekly.

articles.title: See which jobs are most threatened by AI, and who may be able to adapt
articles.author: Kevin Schaul, Shira Ovide
articles.takeaway: Interactive mapping of 350+ occupations by AI exposure and adaptability using GovAI/Brookings research. 6.1M clerical/admin workers most vulnerable (86% women). Consensus: no measurable aggregate displacement yet, but white-collar jobs first in line. Economists stress humility — predictions have historically been poor.

articles.title: Dalende werkgelegenheid onder Nederlandse jongeren die concurreren met GenAI
articles.author: J. Groenewegen, N. van Limbergen, N. Vrieselaar
articles.takeaway: Dutch youth employment in GenAI-vulnerable occupations fell 13% from Q4 2022 to Q3 2025, while other occupations rose 3%. Job postings in vulnerable occupations down 25% vs <10% elsewhere. ICT sector grew 6.5% but youth employment fell 11%. Mirrors US findings from Brynjolfsson et al. (2025).

articles.title: Productive Individuals Don't Make Productive Firms
articles.author: George Sivulka
articles.takeaway: Individual AI productivity gains (10x) aren't translating to firm-level value. Historical parallel: electrified textile mills saw no output gains for 30 years until factories were redesigned. Proposes 'Institutional Intelligence' framework with 7 pillars for organizational AI adoption.

articles.title: Why the ATM didn't kill bank teller jobs, but the iPhone did
articles.author: David Oks
articles.takeaway: ATMs didn't reduce bank teller employment due to complementarity, but iPhones/mobile banking caused a 51% collapse (332K to 164K, 2010-2022). Task automation within existing paradigms rarely displaces; paradigm replacement does. AI is still in the 'slotting in' phase.

articles.title: Research on AI and the labor market is still in the first inning
articles.author: Jed Kolko
articles.takeaway: Evidence on AI labor impact is inconclusive; disruption pace matches prior tech transitions. Under 1/5 of firms using AI per Census BTOS.

articles.title: Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence
articles.author: Massenkoff, McCrory
articles.takeaway: New 'observed exposure' metric combining LLM capability with real usage. No systematic unemployment rise, but young worker hiring slowing in exposed occupations.

articles.title: AI Doesn't Reduce Work -- It Intensifies It
articles.author: Ranganathan, Ye
articles.takeaway: Eight-month study of 200 employees found 83% said AI increased their workload through greater pace, scope, and hours -- leading to burnout and cognitive fatigue.

articles.title: Introducing AIR: The AI Resilience Report
articles.author: Jared Chung
articles.takeaway: First canonical aggregator of research on how AI is impacting jobs at the occupational level, with implications and actions for job seekers.

articles.title: What Deindustrialization Did to Men, AI May Do to Women
articles.author: Molly Kinder
articles.takeaway: Millions of women in clerical and customer service roles face AI exposure, echoing the pattern of manufacturing's toll on men during deindustrialization.

articles.title: AI is simultaneously aiding and replacing workers, wage data suggest
articles.author: J. Scott Davis
articles.takeaway: Employment declined 1% since late 2022 in the 10% of sectors most exposed to AI. Wages in AI-exposed sectors rising faster, suggesting augmentation and displacement happening simultaneously.

articles.title: Earnings Season Takeaways: AI-nxiety
articles.author: Goldman Sachs Research
articles.takeaway: No meaningful relationship between productivity and AI adoption economy-wide, but companies that quantified task-level AI productivity saw a median 30% gain.

articles.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of AI
articles.author: Brynjolfsson, Chandar, Chen
articles.takeaway: Overall employment growing robustly, but 22-25 year olds' employment stagnant since late 2022. AI-exposed jobs driving the decline for young workers.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence: friend or foe for hiring in Europe today?
articles.author: ECB
articles.takeaway: Two-thirds of 3,500 euro-area firms use AI. Companies with frequent AI use are 4% more likely to hire additional staff. Only 15% cite reducing labour costs as a factor.

articles.title: The 2026 Global Intelligence Crisis
articles.author: Frank Flight
articles.takeaway: Little evidence of AI disruption in labor data. Forward-looking labor market components have improved. AI data center construction driving a pick-up in construction hiring.

articles.title: Firm Data on AI
articles.author: Bloom, Barrero, Davis et al.
articles.takeaway: Survey of ~6,000 executives: 90%+ report no employment impact from AI over past 3 years. Firms expect only -0.7% employment reduction over next 3 years (US: -1.2%).

articles.title: How AI is affecting productivity and jobs in Europe
articles.author: Aldasoro, Gambacorta et al.
articles.takeaway: No evidence that AI reduces employment in the short run. AI augments worker output -- enabling faster task completion and better decisions -- without displacing labour.

articles.title: AI, Productivity, and Labor Markets: A Review of the Empirical Evidence
articles.author: ICLE
articles.takeaway: Comprehensive review: 35.9% of US workers used generative AI by December 2025. Adoption accelerating but unevenly distributed across industries and skill levels.

articles.title: Measuring US workers' capacity to adapt to AI-driven job displacement
articles.author: Manning, Aguirre, Muro, Methkupally
articles.takeaway: Of 37.1 million workers in the top quartile of AI exposure, 26.5 million are in occupations with above-median adaptive capacity. Not all exposed workers are equally vulnerable.

articles.title: The Projected Impact of Generative AI on Future Productivity Growth
articles.author: Arnon, Smetters
articles.takeaway: ~10% of US work affected short-term. AI will boost productivity and GDP by 1.5% by 2035. Jobs AI can completely replace saw 0.75% employment fall 2021-2024.

articles.title: The Iceberg Index: Measuring Skills-centered Exposure in the AI Economy
articles.author: MIT / Oak Ridge National Laboratory
articles.takeaway: AI can already replace 11.7% of the US workforce ($1.2T in wages). Tech layoffs represent just 2.2% of total wage exposure -- the visible tip of the iceberg.

articles.title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
articles.author: Daron Acemoglu
articles.takeaway: AI will increase TFP by only 0.53-0.66% over 10 years. Much less transformative than the hype suggests, because AI can only automate a fraction of tasks in most occupations.

articles.title: Is AI Already Replacing Jobs? A Large-Scale Survey
articles.author: Bick, Blandin, Deming
articles.takeaway: 37.4% of US workers used AI on the job in the past week. Adoption highest among college-educated (52%) and workers earning $100K+ (58%). Survey of 25,000 workers.
